---
title: "From outcomes to distributions"
---

In the foundations module, an outcome represented one complete result of an observation process. For the pronoun example, the outcomes were the forms *he*, *him*, *they*, and *them*. But an analysis might concern only the case or number of the observed form.

A random variable extracts that property. If $X$ records case, then

$$
X(\textit{he})=\text{nominative}
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
X(\textit{him})=\text{accusative}.
$$

Several outcomes may map to the same value. The probability assigned to a value of $X$ is the probability of all outcomes that map to that value. This is how a probability measure on linguistic outcomes induces a distribution over case labels, counts, durations, formant values, or any other represented measurement.

## Random variables

We begin with [why we use random variables](why-random-variables.qmd), then [define a random variable](defining-random-variables.qmd) as a measurable function from outcomes to values. The measurability requirement ensures that the probability of a value can be calculated from an event in the original sample space.

A [discrete random variable](discrete-random-variables.qmd) has separate values that can be listed. Its [probability mass function](probability-mass-functions.qmd) assigns probability to each value. A [continuous random variable](continuous-random-variables.qmd) takes values over an interval, and a [probability density function](probability-density-functions.qmd) represents probabilities as areas rather than probabilities at individual points. A [cumulative distribution function](cumulative-distribution-functions.qmd) applies to either case by assigning a probability to the event that the random variable is less than or equal to a threshold.

## Summaries of a distribution

Once a distribution has been defined, we can ask about its center and spread. The [expected value](expected-values.qmd) is a probability weighted average when that average exists. [Expectations of functions](expectation-of-functions.qmd) allow us to average transformed values, and [linearity of expectation](linearity-of-expectation.qmd) determines the expectation of a sum. Some distributions have no finite expectation, as discussed in [when expectations fail](when-expectations-fail.qmd).

[Variance](variance-and-covariance.qmd) is the expected squared distance from the mean. [Standard deviation](standard-deviation.qmd) expresses that spread in the units of the random variable, while [central moments](central-moments.qmd) extend the same calculation to other powers of the distance from the mean.

The [chapter dependency graph](../learning-path.qmd) links these definitions to the probability concepts they require. Begin with [why we use random variables](why-random-variables.qmd).
